common_name: Peeping Tom Daffodil (Historic Cyclamineus Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; introduced in 1913, Peeping Tom was one of the first Cyclamineus hybrids and remains a benchmark for the strongly reflexed, windswept flower form of that group.

directions: Plant bulbs 4 to 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, spacing them close together for the drift effect this dwarf trumpet daffodil is prized for. Each stem carries a single, strongly swept-back golden-yellow flower with a long, slightly flared trumpet, opening early in the season ahead of most large trumpet cultivars. Peeping Tom multiplies readily where drainage is good and has proven one of the most persistent, long-lived Cyclamineus daffodils in cultivation over a century after its introduction. Leave foliage undisturbed until it yellows naturally to keep clumps vigorous for years of bloom.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit plants

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Rapture is a Wister Award-winning Cyclamineus daffodil valued for its shapely, all-yellow, strongly reflexed flowers.

directions: Set bulbs 4 to 6 inches deep in well-drained soil where plants get at least a half day of direct sun. Rapture produces a single, all-golden-yellow flower per stem with narrow, dramatically swept-back petals and a long, slim, slightly twisted trumpet, giving it a windblown look distinct from broader-cupped daffodils. It earned the American Daffodil Society Wister Award for its outstanding garden performance and reliable, floriferous return year after year. Let the foliage die back naturally before removing it so the bulb can rebuild reserves for the following spring.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit plants

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Segovia is a miniature small-cupped daffodil bred by Alec Gray and honored with both the RHS Award of Garden Merit and the ADS Wister Award.

directions: Plant bulbs 3 to 4 inches deep and space them closely in gritty, well-drained soil, since this dwarf miniature is best appreciated massed in a rock garden, trough, or the front of a border. Each slender stem holds one lightly fragrant flower with reflexed white petals surrounding a shallow, pale lemon-yellow cup that fades to cream as it ages. Segovia blooms in mid-spring and has proven a dependable perennializer for a miniature daffodil, unlike many small hybrids that dwindle after a year or two. Avoid heavy, poorly drained soils, which shorten the life of this and most miniature narcissus cultivars.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit plants

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Accent is a Grant Mitsch-bred, Wister Award-winning large-cupped daffodil noted as one of the best pink-cupped garden cultivars.

directions: Plant bulbs 6 inches deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade. Accent carries broad, overlapping ivory-white perianth segments around a flared, frilled cup of deep salmon-pink, one of the cleanest pink-and-white contrasts among mid-twentieth-century daffodil breeding lines descended from Mrs. R. O. Backhouse. It blooms in mid to late spring on strong, sturdy stems that hold up well through wind and rain, and it has remained in commerce for decades on the strength of its garden performance. Divide congested clumps once flowering declines, replanting promptly so bulbs do not dry out for long.

common_name: Chivalry Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Chivalry is a 1943 Jesse Wills introduction that won the American Dykes Medal in 1947 for its clear medium-blue color and ruffled form.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil, since standing moisture causes rot far more readily than this iris is troubled by drought. Chivalry bears large, ruffled, fragrant flowers of a clear, bright medium blue with an orange beard that shifts to blue at the tip, a color and form combination that earned it the Dykes Medal in 1947 and made it an influential parent behind many later blue bearded iris cultivars. It blooms in midseason on strong, well-branched stalks. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the older woody center and replanting healthy outer fans.

common_name: Helen McGregor Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Light Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Helen McGregor, registered in 1943, won the American Dykes Medal in 1949 for its clear light blue, heavily ruffled flowers.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Helen McGregor bears large flowers of clear, pale blue with heavily ruffled standards and falls and an almost white beard, a refined color and form combination that won the Dykes Medal in 1949 and kept it in wide cultivation for decades afterward. It blooms in midseason and is noted for a light, pleasant fragrance. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor and flowering.

common_name: Blue Rhythm Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Cornflower Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; introduced in 1945, Blue Rhythm won the American Dykes Medal in 1950 and became one of the most influential blue bearded iris parents of its era.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil, since standing moisture causes rot far more readily than this iris is troubled by drought. Blue Rhythm carries very large, softly silvered cornflower-blue flowers with arched, domed standards and semi-flaring falls marked by a bright golden beard frosted white at the tip, along with a light lemon fragrance. Its combination of vigor, floriferous habit, and clear color made it a benchmark blue iris for a generation of hybridizers after it won the Dykes Medal in 1950. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, replanting only firm, healthy fans.

common_name: Babbling Brook Bearded Iris (Dykes Medal-Winning Keppel Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; bred by Keith Keppel and registered in 1965, Babbling Brook won the American Dykes Medal in 1972 for its luminous light blue flowers.

directions: Set rhizomes horizontally with the top surface exposed to the sun, never buried, in well-drained soil; soggy conditions cause rot far more readily than this iris is bothered by drought. Babbling Brook bears a light blue self with a fine diamond-dust sheen and subtle darker veining, topped with a fluffy white beard that turns gold in the throat, on tall, well-branched midseason stalks. Bred by Keith Keppel, it won the Dykes Medal in 1972 and remains one of the more widely available historic light blue tall bearded cultivars. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, discarding the old woody center and replanting healthy outer fans.
